young.html: About 2,300 years ago, in the city of Alexandria in Egypt, a teacher named Euclid wrote a book about shapes. He started with a few things everyone agrees on, like you can draw a straight line from any point to any other point. Then, step by step, he proved hundreds of new facts. Each step used only the facts before it.

His book, the Elements, was used to teach geometry for more than 2,000 years. Some people say it has been copied and printed more than any other book except the Bible. Nobody can count that for sure, but it was the main math book in schools for a very long time.
A proof is a chain of reasons. Each link must hold, and nothing can be taken on trust except the few starting rules Euclid wrote down at the beginning.

young.name: gb-euclid-i1
young.cap: Euclid's very first proof: how to make a triangle with three equal sides using only a straightedge and a compass. Press Next step.

young.html: Make Euclid's triangle with string. You need two pencils, a piece of string and paper. Draw a line AB. Tie the string to a pencil and hold the other end on A, so the string reaches exactly to B. Swing a circle. Do the same from B. Where the two circles cross, mark C. Join C to A and to B. Measure the three sides. Why must they be equal?

Euclid's most famous proof is near the end of his first book. If a triangle has a square corner, the squares built on its two short sides add up to the square on its long side. A 3, 4, 5 triangle works: 9 + 16 = 25. Builders have used that trick to make square corners for a very long time.

full.html: Euclid taught in Alexandria around 300 BC, in the years after Alexander the Great, when the new Greek kings of Egypt were filling the city with scholars. We know almost nothing else about his life. Later writers tell a few stories, but they wrote centuries afterward.

The problem Euclid faced was not a lack of geometry. Greek mathematicians had found a great many results over the previous 250 years, and Egyptian and Babylonian scribes had used practical rules for far longer. The problem was order. Which facts depend on which? What do you have to assume? Euclid gathered the known results into one chain, starting from a small set of definitions, postulates and common notions, and proved everything else from them.

The axiomatic method. State your definitions and assumptions at the start. Then accept nothing else without proof. Each proposition may use only the starting points and the propositions already proved.

full.text:
1. A point is that which has no part.

2. A line is breadthless length.

Let the following be postulated: 1. To draw a straight line from any point to any point. 2. To produce a finite straight line continuously in a straight line. 3. To describe a circle with any centre and distance. 4. That all right angles are equal to one another. 5. That, if a straight line falling on two straight lines make the interior angles on the same side less than two right angles, the two straight lines, if produced indefinitely, meet on that side on which are the angles less than the two right angles.
full.author: Euclid
full.work: Elements, Book I, Definitions 1–2 and the Postulates
full.note: The first two of 23 definitions, then all five postulates.

full.html: Postulates 1 to 3 describe the two tools allowed: a straightedge (to draw and extend lines) and a compass (to draw circles). The fifth, the parallel postulate, is longer and less obvious than the rest. Euclid held it back until Proposition 29, as if he used it only when he had to.

full.name: gb-euclid-i1
full.cap: Drag A or B, then step through the construction. Each step names the postulate or definition it rests on.

full.text:
On a given finite straight line to construct an equilateral triangle.

Let AB be the given finite straight line. Thus it is required to construct an equilateral triangle on the straight line AB. With centre A and distance AB let the circle BCD be described; again, with centre B and distance BA let the circle ACE be described; and from the point C, in which the circles cut one another, to the points A, B let the straight lines CA, CB be joined.
full.author: Euclid
full.note: The statement and the construction; the proof that follows shows each side equals AB.

full.html: Notice the pattern every proposition follows: a statement of what is to be done or proved, a figure with lettered points, the construction, the proof with a reason for each step, and the closing words: being what it was required to do (for a construction) or what it was required to prove (for a theorem). Later readers shortened the Latin form of the second to Q.E.D.

full.text: What Books I to IV contain

head: Book
Subject
A landmark
rows: I.32: the angles of a triangle make two right angles; I.47: the Pythagorean theorem
II.4: the square on a whole line equals the squares on its two parts plus twice the rectangle on them, our $(a+b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2$
III.31: an angle in a semicircle is right
Polygons drawn in and around circles
IV.11: the regular pentagon; IV.16: the regular 15-sided figure
full.cap: Books I to IV are the plane geometry most schools still teach.

full.text: The theorem at the end of Book I
In right-angled triangles the square on the side subtending the right angle is equal to the squares on the sides containing the right angle.
full.author: Euclid

full.html: Euclid means real squares with real areas, not numbers. His proof draws a line from the right angle straight down through the big square, cutting it into two rectangles, and shows that each rectangle has the same area as one of the small squares. The visual below shows the same equality by sliding the squares, using two facts Euclid proves earlier: parallelograms on the same base and between the same parallels are equal in area (I.35), and a triangle is half of a parallelogram with the same base and height (I.41).

full.name: gb-euclid-i47
full.cap: Drag the corner A around the half circle, then play the three moves. Each move keeps the area the same.

full.title: A ladder and a wall
full.q: A ladder 13 feet long leans against a wall with its foot 5 feet from the wall. How high up the wall does it reach?
steps: The wall and the ground make a right angle, so the ladder is the side opposite the right angle.

full.title: The third angle
full.q: Two angles of a triangle are 48° and 71°. What is the third, and what is the exterior angle beside it?
steps: By I.32 the three angles make two right angles: 180°.
The exterior angle next to it is $180 - 61 = 119$ degrees, which is also $48 + 71$, the two opposite interior angles (also I.32).

full.html: Thinking Euclid invented all of this. The Pythagorean theorem was known long before Pythagoras: a Babylonian clay tablet from about 1800 BC (Plimpton 322) lists sets of numbers like 3, 4, 5 that fit it. Euclid's own contribution was the order and the proofs. Another slip: "Q.E.D." is not in Euclid. It is the Latin shortening, used by later editors, of his closing Greek phrase.

full.text: What later mathematics kept, and what it changed

items: Kept: almost every result in Books I to IV, the idea of proof from stated assumptions, and the compass-and-straightedge constructions still taught in school.
Repaired: Euclid sometimes relied on a figure. In I.1 he never proves that the two circles actually cross. In 1899 David Hilbert rewrote the foundations with a longer, complete list of axioms.

Changed: in the 1820s and 1830s Nikolai Lobachevsky and János Bolyai showed that a consistent geometry can be built with the parallel postulate replaced (Gauss had reached the same idea privately). Einstein's general relativity (1915) describes space-time with such curved geometry.

deep.html: For two thousand years mathematicians tried to prove the parallel postulate from the other four, Ptolemy and Proclus among them, and later Islamic mathematicians such as Omar Khayyam and Nasir al-Din al-Tusi, and the Italian Girolamo Saccheri (1733). Each attempt either failed or quietly assumed something equal to it. The eventual answer was surprising: it can't be proved, because geometries where it is false are just as consistent.

This changed how mathematicians think about axioms. They are no longer "self-evident truths" about space but chosen starting points. Which geometry describes the real world is a question for measurement, not for logic alone.

No copy from Euclid's time survives. Our text comes from medieval Greek manuscripts (the oldest dated one, at Oxford, was copied in AD 888), from Arabic translations made in Baghdad around AD 800, and from Latin translations made from the Arabic and the Greek in the 1100s. Small papyrus scraps from Roman Egypt show that the text was much the same in about AD 100. The first printed edition came out in Venice in 1482. The standard Greek text today is J. L. Heiberg's (1883–1888), which Heath translated.

Readers have argued about the story that King Ptolemy asked Euclid for an easier way and was told there is "no royal road" to geometry. It comes from Proclus, writing about 750 years later, and a nearly identical story is told of another mathematician and Alexander the Great. Treat it as a legend about the subject, not a fact about the man.

items: Is a proof that relies on a picture really a proof?
Why does a list of five postulates produce so much? Could a different list produce a different world?
Many people, from Abraham Lincoln to Bertrand Russell, said studying Euclid taught them what it means to prove something. What does a proof give you that a measurement can't?

deep.html: Later books on this ladder answer Euclid directly. Spinoza wrote his Ethics in Euclid's form, with definitions, axioms and propositions. Descartes joined geometry to algebra. Newton set out the Principia as propositions with proofs, in Euclid's manner.

questions: Euclid accepted five postulates without proof. What would you put on a list of things "everyone agrees on" about shapes?
Why do you think Euclid's book was used in schools for so long? Is there any book you think will still be read in 2,000 years?
Is it enough to measure a few right triangles and see that the squares add up? What does Euclid's proof give you that measuring doesn't?
The parallel postulate turned out not to be necessary. Can you think of a rule that seemed obvious to you but turned out not to be true everywhere?
Try the string construction together. What could go wrong if the string stretched?
